newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel leader declares "pause" in civil war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader declares "pause" in civil war.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila declared on Thursday a three-day "pause" in the war against the government to give president Mobutu Sese Seko time to consider resignation.

Lubumbashi, the second city and capital of Shaba region, fell to rebels at 2 p.m. local time (1200 GMT) on Wednesday, but rebels had not yet gained control of the airport, Kabila told a news conference.
Kabila stressed the "pause" was not a ceasefire but a slowdown in military operations and said he was optimistic Mobutu would show willingness to negotiate his departure within three days.
"I am waiting for a little period of three days for Mobutu to make a decision to contact us to negotiate his departure," Kabila said at Mobutu's former palace in Goma, now used as rebel headquarters.
Asked whether he was declaring a ceasefire, he said: "No, a pause. I am not saying more. We hope that something big will happen within three days."

Rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire (AFDL) have seized control of almost half of the vast country in under six months, prompting a grave crisis for Mobutu who has ruled since 1965 but is now ailing with cancer.

"Lubumbashi has fallen but we are continuing to clear up the outskirts of the city and still pursuing DSP (Special Presidential Division) troops but at the end of the day the city has fallen," he said.

The rebels seized the diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi on Saturday and were several kilometres short of Kananga, capital of Western Kasai, to which Zairean government troops and former Rwandan government soldiers retreated.
Mobutu sacked prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, a veteran opposition leader, on Wednesday and appointed a senior military commander in his place.

Kabila said he had received signals from Mobutu's entourage of Mobutu's willingness to negotiate but declined to elaborate and said Mobutu should contact him personally by telephone, adding "he knows how."
During the three-day period, Kabila said, he awaited "good news on the willingness of Mobutu to depart to the north. If this doesn't happen we will be forced to advance on all fronts."
The news conference followed an evening meeting of senior Alliance military and civilian leaders during called to discuss how best to use the fall of Lubumbashi.
Kabila's forces took the diamond hub of Mbuji-Mayi last week and now hold about half the territory of Africa's third largest nation, including all the mainstay mineral-producing provinces.
They entered Lubumbashi after stiff resistance from Mobutu loyalists on the approaches to the city of one million people.

Kabila, buoyed by what he described as the rebels' greatest victory at Lubumbashi, said the central demands of Zaire rebels remained a summit between Kabila and Mobutu, a one-year transitional period of AFDL control and then a ceasefire.
"Only when Mr Mobutu has decided to give power to the AFDL will the question of a ceasefire be finished," he said.
Kabila also said U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan was mistaken in calling for an immediate ceasefire, arguing Annan was not in a position to teach rebels what to do.
